newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Buba warns Bonn against tricks to enter EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Buba warns Bonn against tricks to enter EMU.

text.p: The Bundesbank warned on Monday Bonn against resorting to tricks designed to squeeze Germany into currency union, standing its ground in a fight over controversial plans to revalue German reserves.

Still angered by Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plan to revalue national gold and currency reserves and use a part of those proceeds to fill budget holes this year, the Bundesbank likened Bonn's plans to practices Bonn itself had abhorred.

"A transfer of funds from a revalution in 1997 could be seen as creative accouting," Bundesbank official Helmut Hesse said in Hanover, recalling Germany's disdain when Italy and France gained approval for one-off measures to meet EMU goals.
Earlier Waigel, eager to defuse the unusally public and bitter row, said he hoped to reach agreement with the central bank, but also said the government would not back off its plan.

"We will discuss this with the Bundesbank," Waigel told reporters, adding that the dispute centred on the question of whether to revalue the reserves in 1997 or 1998. "We will try to do this in mutual agreement."

For the Bundesbank however the more irritating point is Bonn's plan to grab unrealised profits this year, a move many council members likened to an infringement on central bank's hallowed independence.
Bundesbank officials, driving their point home to audiences across Germany, insisted the asset revaluation should only occur once currency union has begun.
For the Bundesbank, any concession on the date when profits might be paid out would be a small but potentially key concession, officials said at a reception in Mainz.
While sticking by its tough talk, the Bundesbank nonetheless appeared interested in finding a solution to the problems which have tarnished Germany's image abroad.
While Waigel said he was seeking agreement with the Bundesbank, he also said he would proceed with Bonn's plan to change the central bank law even without its assent.
Asset revaluation in 1997 could help Germany meet the criteria to qualify for EMU.

Conciliatory sounds from Bonn came amid growing worries about plans for Europe's single currency project, which appeared to have been put in further danger by the swing to the left in Sunday's parliament election in France.
"The outcome of the parliamentary election in France holds the danger that the independence of the future European central bank might be weakened," Hesse said.
The Bundesbank has long demanded the future European central bank be just as independent as the Bundesbank, laying the foundations for a strong currency.

At a reception in Mainz where Bundesbank officials rubbed shoulders with Bank of France president Jean-Claude Trichet, directorate member Edgar Meister, reading from hand-written notes, said the French election outcome had changed the environment for EMU and it might become clear in the next few weeks whether the euro would be a stable currency.
Similarly Bundesbank officials steered clear of appearing to lend Germany a helping hand as government officials try to scrounge for extra funds to gain access to currency union.
Hesse supported a strict interpretation of Maastricht Treaty entry criteria and ruled out any suggestion these might be loosened in order to help Germany enter on time in 1999.
As Bundesbank leaders stepped up their campaign against Bonn's grab for the gold, criticism from newspaper editorials and opposition parties again poured down on the beleaguered finance minister.
Although the government was deeply divided on Monday over Waigel's plans to fill gaping budget holes, Waigel said there was no danger the centre-right coalition would collapse.
The two main opposition parties, the Social Democrats and the Greens, launched a united bid to call for Waigel's dismissal through a parliamentary vote.

Some independent economists have said Waigel could well be manoeuvred out of his job, triggering a huge cabinet shakeup which might leave the junior coalition partner Free Democrats with the finance ministry's main job.
Separately Chancellor Helmut Kohl has underscored the central bank's autonomy, shrugging off suggestion's Waigel's plan had strayed onto sacred territory.

"Let me state here, clearly and categorically: in no way does the revaluation of the Bundesbank reserves amount to an infringement of the independence of the Bundesbank," Kohl said at an economic conference in Switzerland.
He added, nevertheless, that he was ready for reasonable talks with central bank leaders.
